name: Rasagiline (Azilect)
summary: Once-daily MAO-B inhibitor used for Parkinson’s disease. Not a psychiatric medication—but psychiatry-relevant because it can trigger hallucinations, impulse-control problems, sleep attacks, and dangerous serotonin syndrome when mixed with certain antidepressants or opioids.
description: Rasagiline (Azilect) is a Parkinson’s medication that increases dopamine signaling by blocking MAO-B. From a psychiatry lens, the big issues are safety: it can worsen hallucinations, confusion, agitation, impulsive behaviors (like gambling or hypersexuality), and it has high-stakes drug interactions (especially with serotonergic antidepressants, dextromethorphan, certain opioids, and St. John’s wort). It can also cause sudden sleep episodes and blood pressure problems. It’s taken once daily and is usually continued long-term for Parkinson’s—so the medication reconciliation piece matters a lot.
patient_summary: Azilect is for Parkinson’s—not anxiety or depression. But it matters in psychiatry because it can cause hallucinations, impulsive behaviors, and sleep attacks, and it can be dangerous with some antidepressants, opioids, cough meds (dextromethorphan), and St. John’s wort. Tell your prescriber every medication and supplement you take.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Anti-Parkinson Agent, MAO Type B Inhibitor

linked_conditions.context: Used once daily as monotherapy or as add-on treatment. When combined with levodopa, levodopa dose reductions may be needed to prevent worsening dyskinesias.
Can trigger or worsen hallucinations, delusions, confusion, agitation, and psychotic-like symptoms—especially in vulnerable patients or when dopaminergic tone increases.
Dopaminergic therapies used in Parkinson’s have been associated with compulsive behaviors and loss of impulse control (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, uncontrolled spending).
Serotonin syndrome has been reported when combined with serotonergic antidepressants and certain opioids. Medication reconciliation is essential.

contraindications: Concomitant use of any monoamine oxidase inhibitor (including selective MAO-B inhibitors) within 14 days

efficacy_response.patient_text: Rasagiline is not used to treat psychiatric conditions like anxiety, panic, or insomnia. In psychiatry, it mainly matters for safety, behavior changes, and high-risk medication interactions.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Clinical effects relate to irreversible MAO-B inhibition; blood levels peak ~1 hour after a dose, but symptom effects may build over days.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: ~3 hours (does not match biologic effect due to irreversible inhibition)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic N-dealkylation and/or hydroxylation via CYP1A2 to multiple inactive metabolites

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Rasagiline (Azilect) is a Parkinson’s medication—not a psychiatric medication. In psychiatry, it shows up because it can affect mood, thinking, behavior, and sleep, and it can be dangerous with certain antidepressants, opioids, cough medicines, and supplements.

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This isn’t prescribed for anxiety or depression, but people can still feel real brain-and-body effects. Here’s how it tends to show up in real life:

quotes: When my Parkinson’s symptoms were steadier, my mood wasn’t as wrecked.
I felt more like myself when my body wasn’t fighting me all day.
I didn’t feel 'happy' from the pill—life just felt more manageable.
items.note: Any mood benefit is usually indirect (less disability, less stress), not a direct antidepressant effect.

quotes: I got headaches the first week and then it calmed down.
It wasn’t dramatic—just a low-grade 'not great' feeling.
Some days I felt kind of blah and couldn’t tell why.
items.note: Headache is one of the more common side effects.

quotes: I got sleepy out of nowhere.
It felt like my eyelids had weights on them.
The scariest part was realizing I could nod off without warning.
items.note: Sudden sleep episodes can happen—even long after starting.

quotes: I started seeing things in the corner of my eye.
I felt more confused—like my brain was buffering.
My family noticed I was more suspicious and on edge.
items.note: New or worsening hallucinations, delusions, confusion, agitation, and psychotic-like symptoms can occur after starting or increasing dose.

quotes: I felt driven to do things I normally wouldn’t do.
It wasn’t a craving—it was an urge that didn’t feel negotiable.
items.note: Compulsive behaviors (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, uncontrolled spending) have been reported with dopaminergic Parkinson’s therapies.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Rasagiline peaks in the blood about an hour after a dose, but its real effect is tied to irreversible MAO-B inhibition—so the benefit isn’t just about the blood level in that moment.
key_points: ~1 hour: Peak blood level after a dose
~3 hours: Blood half-life (does not predict how long effects last)
~1 week: Biologic effect can persist due to irreversible MAO-B inhibition
Sleepiness can show up early or much later—some cases are reported after a year on treatment

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Rasagiline is not a psychiatric treatment for anxiety, panic, insomnia, or mood disorders. Its psychiatry relevance is primarily safety: mental status changes, hallucinations, impulse-control problems, and serious interactions that can cause serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Do NOT mix rasagiline with certain antidepressants, dextromethorphan cough meds, or specific opioids—serotonin syndrome can be life-threatening.
other: Mental status and behavioral changes: hallucinations, delusions, confusion, disorientation, agitation, delirium, aggressive behavior
Impulse-control problems: compulsive gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, uncontrolled spending, other intense urges
Somnolence and sudden sleep episodes during daily activities (including driving)
Blood pressure problems: can worsen hypertension; rare hypertensive crisis risk with very high-tyramine foods or interacting meds
Orthostatic hypotension (especially with levodopa): dizziness, fainting, falls—most common early in treatment
Dyskinesia may worsen when used with levodopa; levodopa dose reduction may be needed
Melanoma risk: Parkinson’s itself is linked to higher melanoma risk; rasagiline labeling also emphasizes regular skin checks
Abrupt discontinuation of antiparkinsonian therapy can cause a discontinuation syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome
patient_counseling: Before starting, list every medication and supplement you take (including cough/cold meds and herbal products).
If you take antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs or others), your prescriber needs a plan—some combinations are not recommended and may require washout periods.
Avoid dextromethorphan (common in cough syrups) and St. John’s wort.
Do not drive if you feel unusually sleepy, and tell your prescriber immediately if you fall asleep without warning.
Stand up slowly, especially early in treatment, and report fainting or frequent dizziness.
If new hallucinations, paranoia, agitation, or 'out of character' behaviors show up, report it fast—dose changes or stopping may be needed.

Ask for guidance about high-tyramine foods (aged cheeses, cured meats, draft beers, certain fermented products)—at recommended doses most people don’t need a full tyramine-restricted diet, but very high tyramine can be risky.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common reported side effect is headache. Psychiatry-relevant effects include hallucinations, confusion, agitation, impulse-control problems, depression symptoms, and sudden sleep episodes.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or falling asleep without warning
Hallucinations or confusion (especially in vulnerable patients)
Dizziness or lightheadedness when standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Falls (especially if combined with levodopa or low blood pressure)

common.patient_note: Headaches can happen, especially early. If headaches are severe, persistent, or come with very high blood pressure symptoms (severe headache + chest pain + sweating), treat that as urgent.
Mood changes can show up in Parkinson’s for many reasons (disease, stress, meds). If depression worsens, or if suicidal thoughts appear, that’s a same-day call to your prescriber.
Seeing or hearing things that aren’t there, or feeling paranoid/confused, can be medication-related—especially when dopaminergic tone increases. Don’t wait this out if it’s new.
Orthostatic hypotension can make you dizzy when you stand. This is most common early and can improve over time, but falls are a serious risk—especially in older adults or with levodopa.
Sleepiness can be subtle or abrupt. If you fall asleep during activities like driving, eating, or talking, the medication often needs to be stopped.

serious: Serotonin syndrome (especially with serotonergic antidepressants or certain opioids): agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, diarrhea—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Hypertensive crisis (rare, higher risk with interacting meds or very high-tyramine foods): severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Severe mental status changes: delirium, paranoia, psychotic symptoms, aggressive behavior—urgent evaluation.
Impulse-control disorder behaviors (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, uncontrolled spending) that can seriously damage relationships and finances.
Antiparkinsonian discontinuation syndrome (abrupt stop): fever, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: This is where psychiatry needs to be extra careful. Rasagiline is an MAO-B inhibitor at recommended doses, and it can become less selective at higher doses. Mixing it with certain meds can trigger serotonin syndrome or dangerous blood pressure spikes.

items.with: Other MAO inhibitors (including selective MAO-B inhibitors)
items.risk: Serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis risk; dangerous excess monoamine effects.
Serious reactions including serotonin syndrome; potentially life-threatening.
Serotonin syndrome risk and severe CNS toxicity.
Serious CNS and serotonergic toxicity risk.
Serotonergic toxicity risk and unpredictable interactions.
Serotonin syndrome has been reported; risk varies by agent and dose, and labeling differs by country.
items.action: Concomitant use is not recommended; if switching, allow washout time. Extra caution with long half-life meds like fluoxetine (longer washout may be needed).

items.risk: More dopaminergic side effects including dyskinesia and possibly hallucinations/behavior changes.
items.action: Levodopa dose reduction may be needed to avoid worsening dyskinesias; monitor closely for neuropsychiatric side effects.

items.risk: May increase rasagiline levels, increasing side effects (including sleepiness and blood pressure issues).
items.action: Use caution; monitor for excessive side effects and consider dose adjustment if clinically indicated.

items.with: High-tyramine foods (aged cheeses, cured meats, some fermented products, draft beer)
items.risk: At recommended doses most people don’t need full tyramine restriction, but very high tyramine intake can trigger severe hypertension.
items.action: Avoid foods with very high tyramine content (>150 mg). Food freshness matters—spoiled or improperly stored foods can concentrate tyramine.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Rasagiline isn’t a benzo and doesn’t have the same kind of withdrawal story, but abruptly stopping antiparkinsonian therapy can still be dangerous. Sudden interruption has been associated with a discontinuation syndrome that can resemble neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, severe rigidity, confusion, and autonomic instability).
key_points: Do not stop suddenly unless your prescriber tells you to—especially if you’re on multiple Parkinson’s meds.
If the medication is being stopped due to hallucinations, agitation, or confusion, your prescriber may adjust other dopaminergic meds at the same time.
If you develop high fever, severe stiffness/rigidity, confusion, or severe blood pressure instability after stopping, seek emergency care.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: This medication is dosed for Parkinson’s disease, not for psychiatric conditions like anxiety or insomnia. Psychiatry-relevant dosing is mainly about interaction safety and dose limits in liver impairment.

adult.interaction_safety_note: High-risk interactions exist (especially serotonergic antidepressants, dextromethorphan, certain opioids, and St. John’s wort). Medication reconciliation is essential before starting or changing therapy.
adult.hepatic_limit: Mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh 5 to 6): do not exceed 0.5 mg PO once daily; moderate to severe impairment (Child-Pugh 7 to 15): use is not recommended.

sections.simple_explanation: Rasagiline is usually taken once daily. Even though its blood half-life is short, it works by irreversibly blocking MAO-B, so its biologic effect lasts much longer. The biggest dosing issue in psychiatry is not 'how much for anxiety'—it’s whether it’s safe to combine with other meds.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Human pregnancy and breastfeeding data are limited. When mental status changes or sleep attacks occur, older adults and medically complex patients can be at higher risk of harm (falls, confusion, accidents).
sections.pregnancy: Limited human data. Animal studies showed adverse effects. If used in pregnancy, it should be because the clinical need is clear and alternatives are not appropriate, with close monitoring and coordination across neurology, obstetrics, and psychiatry when relevant.
sections.lactation: It is not known whether rasagiline is present in breast milk. The manufacturer recommends weighing infant exposure risk against the benefits of breastfeeding and benefits of treatment to the mother.
sections.pediatrics: Not applicable for this medication in typical psychiatric practice.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Monitor closely for orthostatic hypotension, falls, hallucinations/confusion, impulse-control behaviors, and daytime sleepiness.
sections.hepatic: Mild impairment (Child-Pugh 5 to 6): maximum 0.5 mg once daily. Moderate to severe impairment (Child-Pugh 7 to 15): use not recommended due to markedly increased exposure.
sections.renal: Mild to moderate impairment: no dosage adjustment necessary. Severe impairment: not studied; use clinical judgment and monitor.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Blood pressure: baseline, periodically, and as clinically indicated (watch for sustained hypertension or symptomatic orthostasis).
Mental status and behavior: hallucinations, paranoia, delusions, confusion, agitation, delirium—especially after starting or dose increases.
Impulse-control symptoms: gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive spending, other intense urges; ask directly and nonjudgmentally.
Somnolence and sleep attacks: daytime sleepiness, nodding off without warning; assess driving safety and other high-risk activities.
Falls risk: especially early treatment and in combination with levodopa; evaluate orthostatic vitals and environmental risks.
Skin exams: regular checks for melanoma (Parkinson’s disease itself is associated with higher melanoma risk; labeling also emphasizes screening).
Liver and renal function: baseline and as clinically indicated, especially if hepatic impairment is known or suspected.
Medication reconciliation: every visit—specifically screen for serotonergic antidepressants, opioids, cough/cold products, and supplements like St. John’s wort.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Rasagiline is taken by mouth once daily and can be taken with or without food.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Rasagiline is a potent, irreversible, selective inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) in the brain. MAO-B breaks down dopamine. By inhibiting MAO-B, rasagiline reduces dopamine breakdown and supports dopamine signaling. That’s useful for Parkinson’s symptoms—but increased dopaminergic tone can also raise the risk of hallucinations, impulsive behaviors, and other neuropsychiatric side effects in some patients.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, rasagiline is mostly a 'med list landmine' medication: it’s not prescribed for anxiety, panic, or insomnia, but it changes what is safe to prescribe. If a patient is on rasagiline, you have to think carefully about serotonergic antidepressants, certain opioids, cough suppressants (dextromethorphan), and supplements. It can also complicate the picture when someone presents with hallucinations, confusion, agitation, or risky impulsive behaviors—because the medication may be contributing, especially alongside levodopa or other dopaminergic therapies.

seo.title: Rasagiline (Azilect): Interactions, Side Effects, Serotonin Syndrome Risk
seo.description: Azilect (rasagiline) is a Parkinson’s MAO-B inhibitor. Psychiatry-relevant risks: hallucinations, confusion, impulse-control behaviors, sleep attacks, and dangerous interactions with antidepressants, opioids, dextromethorphan, and St. John’s wort.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: Is rasagiline (Azilect) used for anxiety, depression, or insomnia?
faqs.a: No. Rasagiline is a Parkinson’s medication. It’s not a treatment for anxiety, panic, insomnia, or depression. In psychiatry, it matters because it can affect thinking and behavior (hallucinations, confusion, agitation, impulse-control issues) and because it has high-risk drug interactions.

faqs.q: Why do psychiatrists care about Azilect if it’s a Parkinson’s medication?
faqs.a: Because it’s an MAO-B inhibitor. That changes what’s safe to prescribe. Mixing it with certain antidepressants, cough suppressants (dextromethorphan), specific opioids, or St. John’s wort can trigger serotonin syndrome or dangerous blood pressure spikes. It can also worsen hallucinations or impulsive behaviors in some people.

faqs.q: Can I take SSRIs or SNRIs with rasagiline?
faqs.a: This is a high-caution situation. Serotonin syndrome has been reported with concomitant antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, and others), and some labeling recommends avoiding the combination or using washout periods. If you’re on an antidepressant—or planning to start one—your prescriber needs to coordinate the plan and timing carefully. Never make this switch on your own.

faqs.q: What medications are absolutely unsafe with rasagiline?
faqs.a: Avoid/contraindicated combinations include other MAO inhibitors, dextromethorphan, cyclobenzaprine, St. John’s wort, and certain opioids (including meperidine, methadone, tramadol, and propoxyphene). Always double-check cough/cold products—dextromethorphan is very common.

faqs.q: Can rasagiline cause hallucinations or confusion?
faqs.a: Yes. New or worsening hallucinations, delusions, confusion, disorientation, agitation, and even delirium have been reported—sometimes after starting or increasing the dose. If this shows up, your prescriber may need to reduce the dose, adjust other Parkinson’s meds, or stop rasagiline.

faqs.q: What are impulse-control problems and why do they matter here?
faqs.a: Impulse-control problems are behaviors that feel driven and hard to resist—like gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, uncontrolled spending, or other intense urges. Dopaminergic Parkinson’s therapies have been linked to these behaviors. If you or your family notices sudden ‘out of character’ behaviors, tell the prescriber right away.

faqs.q: What is serotonin syndrome and what should I watch for?
faqs.a: Serotonin syndrome is a dangerous medication reaction that can happen when serotonergic meds are combined in unsafe ways. Warning signs can include agitation, confusion, fever, sweating, diarrhea, tremor, muscle stiffness, and fast heart rate. If you suspect it, seek emergency care.

faqs.q: Do I need to avoid tyramine foods on rasagiline?
faqs.a: At recommended doses, most people don’t need a strict tyramine-restricted diet. But very high tyramine foods can still be risky. Aged cheeses, cured meats, draft beers, and some fermented products can be high in tyramine—especially if food is spoiled or improperly stored. If you get sudden severe headache or very high blood pressure symptoms, treat it as urgent.

faqs.q: Can rasagiline make you sleepy or cause ‘sleep attacks’?
faqs.a: Yes. Somnolence and falling asleep during daily activities (including driving) have been reported, sometimes without warning. If you have significant daytime sleepiness or any episode of falling asleep during activities, your prescriber will usually recommend stopping the medication and avoiding driving.

faqs.q: What happens if I stop rasagiline suddenly?
faqs.a: Don’t stop suddenly unless your prescriber directs you. Abrupt discontinuation or interruption of antiparkinsonian therapy has been associated with a discontinuation syndrome that can resemble neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability). If severe symptoms happen after stopping, seek emergency care.

For Parkinson’s, it’s typically taken once daily. As monotherapy or as add-on therapy (not including levodopa), the dose is commonly 1 mg once daily (max 1 mg/day). When added to levodopa, it often starts at 0.5 mg once daily and may increase to 1 mg once daily based on response and tolerability (max 1 mg/day). In mild liver impairment, the maximum is 0.5 mg once daily, and it’s not recommended in moderate to severe hepatic impairment.

faqs.q: Is rasagiline safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Human data are limited. Animal studies showed adverse effects. It’s not known whether it passes into breast milk. If pregnancy or breastfeeding is relevant, the decision should be individualized with the prescriber, weighing the benefits to the parent and potential risks to the fetus/infant.
